subChunks.title: Organic Chemistry — Structure, Reactions & Mechanisms

storyBeats.txt: Theodora set a drop of oil and a cup of water side by side. "For much of history," she said, "chemists believed that organic compounds — the molecules of living things — could only be produced by living organisms. They called it the vital force. Then in 1828, Friedrich Wöhler accidentally synthesised urea from inorganic reagents and shattered the boundary between the living and the chemical world forever."

"Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon. Carbon is extraordinary: it forms four strong covalent bonds, bonds happily to itself in chains and rings of any length, and can hold single, double, and triple bonds. From these simple rules emerges the molecular basis of everything biological — proteins, DNA, fats, sugars — and virtually all drugs, plastics, fuels, and dyes."

"The key to organic chemistry is mechanism — not memorising reactions, but understanding why bonds break and form. Electrons move from where they are concentrated to where they are deficient. Master that principle and you can reason through reactions you have never seen before."

subChunks.hookHtml: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-containing compounds — roughly 10 million known compounds, and more synthesised every year. Carbon's unique ability to form four stable covalent bonds, bond to itself, and participate in single, double, and triple bonds generates an almost unlimited diversity of structures. Organic chemistry underlies all of biochemistry, pharmaceuticals, materials science, and petroleum chemistry. Understanding it requires not just knowing reactions but understanding the electronic mechanisms that drive them.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Carbon — The Central Atom

Carbon (atomic number 6, electron configuration 1s²2s²2p²) has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds. Key hybridisations:

  • sp³: Four single bonds, tetrahedral geometry (109.5°). Example: methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆).
  • sp²: Three bonds in a plane (120°), one p orbital perpendicular → forms π bonds (double bonds). Example: ethene (C₂H₄), benzene.
  • sp: Two bonds (180°), two p orbitals → triple bonds. Example: ethyne (C₂H₂).

Functional Groups

Functional groups are characteristic structural units that confer specific chemical properties. Key groups:

  • Alkane (−CH₃, −CH₂−): Only C−H and C−C single bonds. Generally unreactive.
  • Alkene (C=C): Double bond — reactive toward addition reactions.
  • Alkyne (C≡C): Triple bond — very reactive.
  • Alcohol (−OH): Polar, hydrogen-bonding, can be oxidised.
  • Aldehyde (−CHO): Carbonyl at chain end; easily oxidised to carboxylic acid.
  • Ketone (C=O): Carbonyl within chain; harder to oxidise.
  • Carboxylic acid (−COOH): Acidic (pKa ≈ 4–5), forms esters and amides.
  • Amine (−NH₂): Basic, nucleophilic.
  • Ester (−COO−): Formed from acid + alcohol; fats are triesters of glycerol.
  • Amide (−CONH−): Peptide bond in proteins.
  • Halide (−X, X = F, Cl, Br, I): Good leaving groups; reactive in substitution.

Isomerism

Structural isomers: Same molecular formula, different connectivity. Example: butane (straight chain) and isobutane (branched).

Stereoisomers: Same connectivity, different spatial arrangement.

  • Geometric (cis/trans or E/Z) isomers: Arise from restricted rotation around a double bond. Cis = same side; trans = opposite. Example: cis-2-butene vs trans-2-butene — different physical properties, same formula.
  • Optical isomers (enantiomers): Molecules with a chiral carbon (four different groups attached) — non-superimposable mirror images. Rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. Critically important in pharmacology — one enantiomer may be therapeutic, the other toxic (thalidomide).

Reaction Mechanisms — Electronic Movement

Organic mechanisms track electron flow. Arrows show movement of electron pairs (curly arrow notation):

  • Nucleophile: Electron-rich species that attacks electron-deficient centres (e.g. OH⁻, NH₃, CN⁻). Attacks electrophiles.
  • Electrophile: Electron-deficient species that accepts electrons (e.g. H⁺, carbocations, halogen molecules).
  • Leaving group: Species that departs with the bonding electrons (e.g. Cl⁻, Br⁻, H₂O).

Key Reaction Types

Addition reactions (alkenes): The π bond breaks; atoms add across the double bond. Example: HBr addition to ethene: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br. Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon with more H atoms (forming the more stable carbocation intermediate).

Substitution reactions:

  • SN2 (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution): Nucleophile attacks from behind; leaving group departs simultaneously. One step; inverts configuration at the chiral centre. Favoured by primary substrates and strong nucleophiles.
  • SN1 (unimolecular): Two steps — leaving group departs first forming a carbocation; nucleophile attacks. Favoured by tertiary substrates. Gives racemic mixture (attack from both faces).

Elimination reactions: Remove H and leaving group from adjacent carbons to form a double bond. Compete with substitution (higher temperature and bulky base favour elimination).

Oxidation and reduction: Organic oxidation: gain of O or loss of H. Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. Secondary alcohol → ketone. Reduction: gain of H (e.g. NaBH₄ reduces ketones to secondary alcohols).

Aromatic Chemistry

Benzene (C₆H₆) has six π electrons delocalised over a ring — unusually stable ("aromatic stabilisation"). Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) rather than addition to preserve the aromatic system. Key EAS reactions: nitration (with HNO₃/H₂SO₄), halogenation (with AlCl₃ catalyst), Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation.

Substituents on benzene direct further substitution: electron-donating groups (−OH, −NH₂) direct to ortho/para positions; electron-withdrawing groups (−NO₂, −COOH) direct to meta.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a reaction mechanism is in organic chemistry — why it matters to know not just that a reaction happens, but how it happens, step by step.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) can be converted to several different products depending on the reagents used. (1) Name the product and reagents required to oxidise propan-1-ol to propanal (an aldehyde). (2) If oxidation continues, what is the final product? (3) Write the structural formula of the ester formed when propan-1-ol reacts with ethanoic acid (acetic acid). Name this ester. (4) Propan-1-ol can also be dehydrated to form an alkene. Name the alkene formed and the reagent/conditions for dehydration. (5) A student claims that propan-2-ol (not propan-1-ol) would give a different aldehyde on oxidation. Is this correct? Explain.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanal: use acidified potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) with careful distillation to remove the aldehyde as it forms (preventing further oxidation). The solution changes from orange to green as Cr(VI) → Cr(III).

(2) If oxidation continues (reflux with excess K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄): propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH). Primary alcohols → aldehyde → carboxylic acid under full oxidation.

(3) Ester formation (Fischer esterification): propan-1-ol + ethanoic acid → propyl ethanoate + water. CH₃COOH + HOCH₂CH₂CH₃ → CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ + H₂O. Conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat (reflux). The ester is propyl ethanoate (also called propyl acetate).

(4) Dehydration of propan-1-ol: heat with concentrated H₂SO₄ (or Al₂O₃ at 180°C) → propene (CH₂=CHCH₃) + H₂O. The acid protonates the OH to form a good leaving group (H₂O), then elimination occurs.

(5) The student is incorrect about forming a different aldehyde. Propan-2-ol (CH₃CHOHCH₃) is a secondary alcohol. Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones, not aldehydes — the product would be propanone (CH₃COCH₃, acetone), not an aldehyde. Secondary carbons lack the H atom on the carbonyl carbon that defines an aldehyde. Ketones are resistant to further oxidation under normal conditions.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Two pharmaceutical drugs, ibuprofen and thalidomide, both have chiral centres. Ibuprofen is sold as a racemic mixture; thalidomide was historically sold as a racemate with disastrous consequences. (1) Define a chiral centre and explain what makes a carbon chiral. (2) What are enantiomers, and how do they differ in physical and chemical properties? (3) Explain why thalidomide's two enantiomers have different biological effects, and why simply separating the enantiomers would not have solved the problem (hint: consider in vivo interconversion). (4) In drug development, why has single-enantiomer synthesis become important? Give one advantage beyond safety. (5) A molecule of 2-bromobutane (CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃) undergoes SN2 reaction with hydroxide ion. Describe the mechanism and the stereochemical outcome at the chiral carbon.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) A chiral centre (chiral carbon) is a carbon atom bonded to four different substituents — no two the same. The four groups can be arranged in two non-superimposable mirror image configurations (like left and right hands). A carbon bearing four different groups lacks any plane of symmetry.

(2) Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images of the same molecule. In achiral environments, they have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility, spectroscopic data) except for optical rotation — one rotates plane-polarised light clockwise (+, R or d), the other anticlockwise (−, S or l). In chiral environments — including biological systems — they interact differently with enzymes, receptors, and other chiral molecules, producing distinct biological effects.

(3) Thalidomide: the R-enantiomer is teratogenic (causes foetal limb malformations); the S-enantiomer has the intended sedative effect. Even if a pure S-enantiomer preparation had been available, it would not have prevented harm: thalidomide racemises in vivo under physiological pH and temperature — the body interconverts the two enantiomers. Any dose of pure S would generate R within hours. This makes thalidomide intrinsically dangerous in pregnancy regardless of enantiopurity.

(4) Single-enantiomer drugs (chiral switches) offer: (a) Safety — avoiding inactive or harmful enantiomers. (b) Potency — the active enantiomer may be significantly more potent than the racemate, allowing lower doses. (c) Reduced drug interactions — fewer off-target effects from the inactive enantiomer. (d) Patent strategy — companies can re-patent a racemate's single enantiomer (e.g. esomeprazole from omeprazole).

(5) SN2 mechanism: hydroxide ion (nucleophile) attacks the back face of the chiral carbon — the carbon bearing the bromine leaving group. This is a concerted one-step process: the C−Br bond breaks as the C−O bond forms simultaneously. The geometry at the chiral carbon inverts — Walden inversion — the three remaining groups flip like an umbrella turning inside out. If the starting material is R-2-bromobutane, the product is S-2-butanol (and vice versa). SN2 always gives complete inversion of configuration at the reaction centre.
learningObjectives: Identify and name common organic functional groups and predict their chemical reactivity based on electronic properties.
Distinguish types of isomerism (structural, geometric, optical) and explain why chirality matters in biological and pharmaceutical contexts.
Describe the mechanisms of addition, substitution (SN1 and SN2), and elimination reactions using curly arrow electron-movement notation.
Explain aromatic stabilisation in benzene and predict the outcome of electrophilic aromatic substitution with different directing groups.
commonMistakes: Confusing SN1 and SN2 — SN2 is one step (backside attack, inversion), favoured by primary substrates; SN1 is two steps (carbocation intermediate), favoured by tertiary substrates and gives racemisation.
Forgetting that secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones, not aldehydes — secondary carbons cannot form the aldehyde −CHO group because they lack a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon.

Applying Markovnikov's rule incorrectly — H adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens, creating the more stable (more substituted) carbocation intermediate; not simply to whichever carbon is on the left.

Treating all stereoisomers as equivalent — enantiomers have identical physical properties but different optical rotation and biological activity; geometric (cis/trans) isomers differ in physical properties (boiling point, polarity) as well as reactivity.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly names and draws functional groups, identifies isomers, and explains chirality with reference to pharmaceutical examples.
Accurately describes SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with correct stereochemical outcomes (SN2 inversion, SN1 racemisation).
Correctly predicts products of addition, oxidation, esterification, and elimination reactions with appropriate reagents and conditions.
Explains electrophilic aromatic substitution and the directing effects of substituents on benzene.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A problem-solving approach in organic chemistry where a target molecule is mentally deconstructed into simpler precursors by working backwards — each bond disconnection reveals a possible synthetic step. Developed by E.J. Corey (Nobel Prize 1990), it is the formal method for planning multi-step organic syntheses of complex natural products and pharmaceuticals.

Organomagnesium halides (RMgX) — powerful nucleophiles/carbanion equivalents that react with carbonyl compounds to form alcohols. A Grignard reagent converts an aldehyde into a secondary alcohol and a ketone into a tertiary alcohol, making them indispensable for building carbon frameworks in synthesis.

The chemistry of the C=O group — aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides. The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic; nucleophilic addition (by hydrides, Grignard reagents, organolithiums) and nucleophilic acyl substitution (for acid derivatives) are the two dominant reaction classes.

A design philosophy for chemical synthesis minimising waste, toxic reagents, and energy use. The 12 Principles of Green Chemistry (Anastas and Warner, 1998) include atom economy (how much of reactants end up in the product) and catalysis (reducing stoichiometric reagent waste). Increasingly central to pharmaceutical and industrial synthesis.

Nuclear Magnetic Resonance spectroscopy is the primary tool for determining the structure of organic molecules. Protons (¹H) in different chemical environments resonate at different frequencies in a magnetic field — the pattern of signals identifies functional groups and connectivity. The same physical principle underlies MRI in medicine.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following correctly describes the product when a primary alcohol is fully oxidised using excess acidified potassium dichromate?
questions.explanationHtml: Primary alcohols (R−CH₂OH) undergo two-stage oxidation: first to an aldehyde (R−CHO), then to a carboxylic acid (R−COOH). Using excess oxidising agent under reflux drives the reaction to completion — carboxylic acid. Distillation of the aldehyde as it forms (before it is further oxidised) is needed to isolate the aldehyde product. Secondary alcohols (R−CHOH−R') oxidise to ketones and cannot be further oxidised under normal conditions. Tertiary alcohols (no H on the −OH carbon) resist oxidation.

questions.questionHtml: 1-bromobutane (a primary alkyl halide) reacts with hydroxide ion (OH⁻) via SN2 mechanism. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (a tertiary alkyl halide) reacts with the same reagent but via SN1 mechanism. Which statement correctly explains why the reaction pathways differ?
options: SN2 is faster with tertiary substrates because carbocations are more stable; SN1 is faster with primary substrates because there is less steric hindrance

SN2 is favoured for primary substrates because the backside approach of the nucleophile is unhindered; SN1 is favoured for tertiary substrates because the tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups, making ionisation feasible
SN1 and SN2 differ only in temperature — SN1 at high temperature, SN2 at low temperature, regardless of substrate
SN2 requires a strong acid catalyst; SN1 requires a strong base — the difference is purely about reagent type
questions.correctAnswer: SN2 is favoured for primary substrates because the backside approach of the nucleophile is unhindered; SN1 is favoured for tertiary substrates because the tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups, making ionisation feasible
questions.explanationHtml: The key factors are steric accessibility and carbocation stability. SN2: the nucleophile must attack the back face of the carbon bearing the leaving group — bulky substituents block this approach. Primary substrates have minimal steric hindrance, allowing SN2. Tertiary substrates: three alkyl groups block the back face, making SN2 extremely slow. SN1: the rate-determining step is ionisation to form a carbocation. Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by three alkyl groups (hyperconjugation and inductive donation) — tertiary carbocations form readily. Primary carbocations are too unstable to form under normal conditions. Therefore: primary → SN2 preferred; tertiary → SN1 preferred; secondary → competition between pathways depending on conditions.

questions.questionHtml: A student synthesises a drug containing a chiral centre and obtains a racemic mixture. She argues: "Since both enantiomers have the same melting point and NMR spectrum, the racemic mixture is just as pure as the single enantiomer — there's no need to separate them for pharmaceutical use." Evaluate this reasoning.
options: Correct — identical physical properties confirm identical biological activity; enantiomers are chemically equivalent in all environments

Incorrect — while enantiomers share physical properties in achiral environments, biological systems are chiral environments; enzymes, receptors, and transporters are themselves chiral and distinguish enantiomers, which may have different potency, selectivity, or toxicity
Correct — only the absolute configuration label (R or S) differs; this is a notational convention with no physical consequence
Incorrect — NMR cannot distinguish enantiomers but IR spectroscopy always can, so the student's claim about NMR is simply wrong
questions.correctAnswer: Incorrect — while enantiomers share physical properties in achiral environments, biological systems are chiral environments; enzymes, receptors, and transporters are themselves chiral and distinguish enantiomers, which may have different potency, selectivity, or toxicity
questions.explanationHtml: The student's reasoning conflates physical properties in achiral environments with biological activity in chiral environments. Enantiomers do have identical melting points, boiling points, solubility, and NMR spectra in achiral solvents (also identical IR spectra — the IR claim in option D is wrong). However, biological macromolecules — enzymes, receptors, ion channels, transport proteins — are themselves composed of chiral amino acids and sugars, making them chiral selectors. The two enantiomers of a drug may bind to a receptor with vastly different affinities, produce different side-effect profiles, or even be toxic. The thalidomide case (one enantiomer teratogenic) is the historical lesson. Regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA) now require systematic evaluation of both enantiomers for new chiral drugs, and single-enantiomer development is the norm for most new drug candidates.
